claim: The Frizzled and Dachsous-Fat PCP systems are connected through the Spiny-legs isoform of the Prickle-Spiny-legs locus.
source: We have characterized how the Frizzled and Dachsous-Fat PCP systems are connected through the Spiny-legs isoform of the Prickle-Spiny-legs locus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including co-immunoprecipitation experiments and localization studies.

claim: Dachsous can independently interact with Spiny-legs and direct its localization in vivo.
source: Two different components of the Dachsous-Fat system, Dachsous and Dachs, can each independently interact with Spiny-legs and direct its localization in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and localization studies in various mutant backgrounds shown in the manuscript.

claim: Dachs can independently interact with Spiny-legs and direct its localization in vivo.
source: Two different components of the Dachsous-Fat system, Dachsous and Dachs, can each independently interact with Spiny-legs and direct its localization in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and localization studies in various mutant backgrounds shown in the manuscript.

claim: The Frizzled PCP pathway includes the asymmetrically distributed transmembrane proteins Fz and Van Gogh.
source: The Drosophila Fz PCP pathway includes the asymmetrically distributed transmembrane proteins Fz and Van Gogh (Vang, also known as Strabismus), which act together with the cadherin family protein Starry night (Stan, also known as Flamingo) (Figure 1A) (Chae et al., 1999; Goodrich and Strutt, 2011; Park et al., 1994; Shimada et al., 2001; Strutt, 2001; Usui et al., 1999; Vinson and Adler, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these components of the Fz PCP pathway.

claim: The Drosophila Ds-Fat PCP pathway includes the cadherin family proteins Ds and Fat, which interact between neighboring cells.
source: The Drosophila Ds-Fat PCP pathway includes the cadherin family proteins Ds and Fat, which interact between neighboring cells (Ma et al., 2003; Matakatsu and Blair, 2004; Strutt and Strutt, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these components of the Ds-Fat PCP pathway.

claim: Binding between Ds and Fat is modulated by Four-jointed (Fj), a Golgi-localized kinase that phosphorylates their cadherin domains.
source: Binding between Ds and Fat is modulated by Four-jointed (Fj), a Golgi-localized kinase that phosphorylates their cadherin domains (Brittle et al., 2010; Ishikawa et al., 2008; Simon et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature describing the role of Fj in modulating Ds-Fat binding.

claim: Ds and Fj are expressed in opposing gradients, which orient Ds-Fat PCP.
source: Ds and Fj are expressed in opposing gradients, which orient Ds-Fat PCP (Casal et al., 2002; Mao et al., 2006; Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Yang et al., 2002; Zeidler et al., 1999; 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is consistent with expression patterns shown in the manuscript.

claim: V5-tagged Dachs can co-immunoprecipitate Flag-tagged Sple.
source: Indeed, V5-tagged Dachs could co-immunoprecipitate Flag-tagged Sple (Figure 1B, lane 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dachs interacts with Sple through the unique N-terminus of Sple.
source: Dachs and Sple interact through the unique N-terminus of Sple, because Dachs also co-precipitated a construct comprising only the Sple N-terminus (Sple-N), but did not co-precipitate a full length Pk construct (Figure 1B, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing interaction with Sple-N but not Pk.

claim: Dachs does not co-precipitate full length Pk.
source: Dachs and Sple interact through the unique N-terminus of Sple, because Dachs also co-precipitated a construct comprising only the Sple N-terminus (Sple-N), but did not co-precipitate a full length Pk construct (Figure 1B, lanes 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Both Sple and Sple-N interact with Ds-ICD, whereas Pk does not.
source: Both Sple and Sple-N also interacted with Ds-ICD, whereas Pk did not (Figure 1B, lanes 4–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: GFP:Pk was polarized towards the proximal sides of cells in the wing disc, except just anterior to the anterior-posterior compartment boundary where it was polarized towards the anterior sides of cells.
source: Consistent with recent studies examining isoform-specific localization (Ayukawa et al., 2014; Sagner et al., 2012; Strutt et al., 2013), we observed that GFP:Pk was polarized towards the proximal sides of cells, except just anterior to the anterior-posterior compartment boundary, where GFP:Pk was instead polarized towards the anterior sides of cells (Figure 1D,G, 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 1D, 1G, and 2I, and is consistent with prior studies.

claim: GFP:Sple was polarized towards the distal sides of cells throughout the wing disc.
source: By contrast, GFP:Sple was polarized towards the distal sides of cells throughout the wing disc (Figure 1C,E,F, 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 1C, 1E, 1F, and 2I.

claim: The distinct localization of Pk and Sple expressed in wing discs indicates that they can respond to distinct spatial cues.
source: The distinct localization of Pk and Sple expressed in wing discs indicates that they can respond to distinct spatial cues.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed distinct localization patterns of Pk and Sple in wing discs.

claim: In dachs mutant wing discs, GFP:Sple localization became similar to that of Pk throughout most of the developing wing disc: on the proximal side of cells, and in fewer, more discrete puncta.
source: Indeed, GFP:Sple localization was altered, as throughout most of the developing wing disc its localization became similar to that of Pk: on the proximal side of cells, and in fewer, more discrete puncta (Figure 2A,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in dachs mutants shown in Figures 2A and 2I.

claim: In the most proximal part of the wing pouch in dachs mutants, GFP:Sple generally maintained a distal localization.
source: Intriguingly, however, in the most proximal part of the wing pouch, GFP:Sple generally maintained a distal localization (Figure 2B,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in dachs mutants shown in Figures 2B and 2I.

claim: Dachs is required for the distal localization of GFP:Sple throughout most of the wing pouch, but not in the proximal wing.
source: Thus, Dachs is required for the distal localization of GFP:Sple throughout most of the wing pouch, but not in the proximal wing.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential effects of dachs mutation on Sple localization in different regions of the wing pouch.

claim: In ds mutant wing discs, GFP:Sple was in most cases unpolarized, but sometimes partially polarized or polarized in random directions.
source: In ds mutant wing discs, GFP:Sple was in most cases unpolarized (localized to cell membrane on all sides), but sometimes partially polarized (on multiple cell sides but with a clear bias), or polarized in random directions (Figure 2D,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in ds mutants shown in Figures 2D and 2I.

claim: In fat mutant wing discs, GFP:Sple was always observed to have unpolarized membrane localization.
source: Dachs is similarly localized to the membrane in an unpolarized fashion in fat mutants (Mao et al., 2006), and we always observed unpolarized membrane localization of GFP:Sple in fat mutant wing discs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in fat mutants shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In ds dachs and fat dachs double mutants, GFP:Sple reverted to a Pk-like localization, including a proximal, punctate orientation throughout most of the wing pouch, and an anterior orientation near the A-P boundary.
source: In both cases, GFP:Sple reverted to a Pk-like localization, including a proximal, punctate orientation throughout most of the wing pouch, and an anterior orientation near the A-P boundary (Figure 2E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in double mutants shown in Figures 2E-I.

claim: In ds dachs or fat dachs mutant discs, GFP:Sple localization is preferentially proximal even in proximal regions of the wing pouch, where GFP:Sple localization was preferentially distal in dachs mutants.
source: One remarkable feature of ds dachs or fat dachs mutant discs is that GFP:Sple localization is preferentially proximal even in proximal regions of the wing pouch, where GFP:Sple localization was preferentially distal in dachs mutants (Figure 2B,F,H,I).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of localization data in different mutant backgrounds shown in Figures 2B, 2F, 2H, and 2I.

claim: Dachs and Ds each have the ability to independently localize GFP:Sple.
source: This implies that the distal localization of GFP:Sple here in dachs mutants is Ds-dependent, and hence that Dachs and Ds each have the ability to independently localize GFP:Sple.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Sple remains distally localized in proximal regions of dachs mutants but becomes proximally localized in ds dachs double mutants.

claim: GFP:Sple localized proximally in dachs pk mutant wing discs.
source: The observation that GFP:Sple localized proximally in dachs pk mutant wing discs (Figure 3F) indicates that Sple can respond to Pk localization cues even in the absence of Pk.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in dachs pk mutants shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Sple can respond to Pk localization cues even in the absence of Pk.
source: The observation that GFP:Sple localized proximally in dachs pk mutant wing discs (Figure 3F) indicates that Sple can respond to Pk localization cues even in the absence of Pk.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Sple localizes proximally in dachs pk mutants.

claim: Localization of Pk was not visibly altered within larval wing discs by dachs, ds, or fat mutations.
source: Localization of Pk was not visibly altered within larval wing discs by dachs, ds, or fat mutations (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fz-PCP is not required for distal localization of Sple, as GFP:Sple remains preferentially distal in vang mutant wing discs.
source: Fz-PCP is not required for distal localization of Sple, as GFP:Sple remains preferentially distal in vang mutant wing discs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in vang mutants shown in Figure 3G.

claim: pk mutants have a characteristic wing polarity phenotype, in which hairs in much of the wing are mis-oriented away from the wing margin, and wing margin bristles can point proximally.
source: sple mutation does not result in a hair polarity phenotype in the wing, whereas pk mutants have a characteristic wing polarity phenotype, in which hairs in much of the wing are mis-oriented away from the wing margin, and wing margin bristles can point proximally (Figure 4D,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 4D, 4H, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: sple mutation does not result in a hair polarity phenotype in the wing.
source: sple mutation does not result in a hair polarity phenotype in the wing, whereas pk mutants have a characteristic wing polarity phenotype, in which hairs in much of the wing are mis-oriented away from the wing margin, and wing margin bristles can point proximally (Figure 4D,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The pk wing hair polarity phenotype is suppressed by dachs mutation.
source: Indeed, when we tested this by comparing wing hair and bristle orientation in pk versus dachs pk mutants, this suppression was observed (Figure 4C–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data comparing pk and dachs pk mutants shown in Figures 4C-J.

claim: Over-expression of Fat could suppress the pk hair polarity phenotype because over-expression of Fat removes Dachs from the membrane.
source: This result can also explain the observation that over-expression of Fat could suppress the pk hair polarity phenotype (Hogan et al., 2011), because over-expression of Fat removes Dachs from the membrane (Mao et al., 2006), which, as Dachs functions at membranes (Pan et al., 2013; Rauskolb et al., 2011), is functionally equivalent to dachs mutation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that dachs mutation suppresses pk phenotypes, combined with prior knowledge that Fat over-expression removes Dachs from membranes.

claim: ds hair polarity phenotypes are suppressed by dachs.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, ds hair polarity phenotypes are suppressed by dachs (Brittle et al., 2012), and we confirmed that fat wing hair polarity phenotypes (generated using wing-specific RNAi) are also suppressed by dachs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: fat wing hair polarity phenotypes are suppressed by dachs.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, ds hair polarity phenotypes are suppressed by dachs (Brittle et al., 2012), and we confirmed that fat wing hair polarity phenotypes (generated using wing-specific RNAi) are also suppressed by dachs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: fat PCP phenotypes are partially suppressed by sple, including restoration of normal, distally oriented polarity in two regions affected by loss of Fat: near the proximal anterior wing margin, and near the anterior cross-vein.
source: This hypothesis further predicts that fat PCP phenotypes could be suppressed by sple (Figure 4A), and while we did not observe completely normal hair polarity in fat sple wings, we did observe a partial suppression, including restoration of normal, distally oriented polarity in two regions affected by loss of Fat: near the proximal anterior wing margin, and near the anterior cross-vein (Figures 4B,K–N; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data comparing fat and fat sple mutants shown in Figures 4B, 4K-N, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: GFP:Sple localized to the equatorial side of cells within both R3 and R4 at the 5-cell precluster stage of ommatidial formation.
source: GFP:Sple localized to the equatorial side of cells within both R3 and R4, which places it within R4 at the R3-R4 interface (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Equatorial polarization of Sple was disrupted in ds or fat mutants.
source: This equatorial polarization of Sple was disrupted in ds or fat mutants (Figure 5C,E), but was not affected by mutation of dachs (Figure 5B), nor could dachs mutation prevent the mis-localization of Sple in ds or fat (Figure 5D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in ds and fat mutants shown in Figures 5C and 5E.

claim: Equatorial polarization of Sple was not affected by mutation of dachs.
source: This equatorial polarization of Sple was disrupted in ds or fat mutants (Figure 5C,E), but was not affected by mutation of dachs (Figure 5B), nor could dachs mutation prevent the mis-localization of Sple in ds or fat (Figure 5D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in dachs mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claim: dachs mutation could not prevent the mis-localization of Sple in ds or fat mutants.
source: This equatorial polarization of Sple was disrupted in ds or fat mutants (Figure 5C,E), but was not affected by mutation of dachs (Figure 5B), nor could dachs mutation prevent the mis-localization of Sple in ds or fat (Figure 5D,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in ds dachs and fat dachs double mutants shown in Figures 5D and 5F.

claim: GFP:Pk localized to the equatorial side of both R3 and R4 cells.
source: We also examined localization of GFP:Pk within R3 and R4, and found that it too localized to the equatorial side of both cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: In sple mutants, Pk localization is altered such that it becomes partially randomized, resembling Sple localization in fat or ds mutants.
source: In support of this, we found that in sple mutants, Pk localization is altered such that it becomes partially randomized, resembling Sple localization in fat or ds mutants (Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in sple mutants shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Equatorial Pk localization in R3 and R4 depends upon Sple.
source: Thus, equatorial Pk localization in R3 and R4 depends upon Sple.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Pk localization is altered in sple mutants.

claim: In front of the morphogenetic furrow, GFP:Sple accumulates on the equatorial sides of cells, as it does behind the furrow, but Pk:GFP accumulates on the anterior sides of cells.
source: Finally, we observed that in front of the morphogenetic furrow, GFP:Sple and GFP:Pk exhibit distinct localization profiles, with GFP:Sple accumulating on the equatorial sides of cells, as it does behind the furrow, but Pk:GFP accumulating on the anterior sides of cells, which in this region is the side closest to the morphogenetic furrow (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Dachs:GFP and Sple:GFP were polarized towards the anterior sides of cells within A compartments of pleural cells, and towards the posterior sides of cells within P compartments.
source: Dachs:GFP and Sple:GFP were polarized towards the anterior sides of cells within A compartments, and towards the posterior sides of cells within P compartments (Figure 6A,B,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 6A, 6B, and 6H.

claim: Pk:GFP was polarized towards the anterior sides of cells within both A and P compartments of pleural cells.
source: Pk:GFP, by contrast, was polarized towards the anterior sides of cells within both A and P compartments (Figure 6C,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 6C and 6H.

claim: In A compartments of pleural cells, Pk:GFP and Sple:GFP polarize in the same direction, whereas in P compartments they polarize in opposite directions.
source: Thus, in A compartments Pk:GFP and Sple:GFP polarize in the same direction, whereas in P compartments they polarize in opposite directions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed localization patterns of Pk and Sple in A and P compartments.

claim: pk-sple mutants reverse hair polarity within the center of the A compartment, while the P compartment, and the edges of the A compartment, exhibit normal hair polarity.
source: Consistent with prior studies (Lawrence et al., 2004), we observed that pk-sple mutants reverse hair polarity within the center of the A compartment, while the P compartment, and the edges of the A compartment, exhibit normal hair polarity (Figure 7B,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 7B and 7F, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: pk mutant alleles have normal polarity in A compartments, but mostly reversed polarity in the P compartment within pleura.
source: pk mutant alleles have normal polarity in A compartments, but mostly reversed polarity in the P compartment within pleura (Figure 7C), although not in tergites (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 7C and 7G.

claim: sple mutant alleles have normal polarity in the P compartment, and abnormal polarity, including hair reversal but also sideways or swirling hair orientations, within the center of the A compartment.
source: sple mutant alleles have normal polarity in the P compartment, and abnormal polarity, including hair reversal but also sideways or swirling hair orientations, within the center of the A compartment (Figure 7D,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 7D and 7H.

claim: Sple localized normally in pk mutants.
source: In the absence of Pk, cells respond instead to Sple-dependent cues, leading to a reversal of polarity (Sple localized normally in pk mutants, Figure 8I,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in pk mutants shown in Figures 8I and 8K.

claim: Pk was mis-localized within the central region of A compartments of sple mutants.
source: The influence of Pk-Sple on polarity in A compartments is reminiscent of the situation in the eye. Sple, not Pk plays the key role in establishing polarity here, and Pk was mis-localized within the central region of A compartments of sple mutants (Figure 6G,H), hence Sple contributes to localization of Pk here.
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data in sple mutants shown in Figures 6G and 6H.

claim: In fat or ds mutants, hair polarity is disturbed in much of the A and P compartments of the abdomen, although a small region at the front of the A compartment exhibits normal hair polarity.
source: In fat or ds mutants, hair polarity is disturbed in much of the A and P compartments, although a small region at the front of the A compartment exhibits normal hair polarity (Figures 9A,E, 10A,E) (Casal et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 9A, 9E, 10A, and 10E, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Mutation of dachs suppressed the hair polarity phenotypes of fat and ds in A compartments of the abdomen.
source: Moreover, mutation of dachs suppressed the hair polarity phenotypes of fat and ds in A compartments (Figures 9C,F, 10C,G) (Mao et al., 2006), and also suppressed the mis-localization of Sple (Figures 6F,H, 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 9C, 9F, 10C, and 10G, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Mutation of dachs suppressed the mis-localization of Sple in fat and ds mutants in A compartments of the abdomen.
source: Moreover, mutation of dachs suppressed the hair polarity phenotypes of fat and ds in A compartments (Figures 9C,F, 10C,G) (Mao et al., 2006), and also suppressed the mis-localization of Sple (Figures 6F,H, 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 6F, 6H, and 8D.

claim: Mutation of dachs alone does not disrupt polarity in A compartments of the abdomen.
source: Mutation of dachs alone does not disrupt polarity in A compartments (Figures 9B, 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 9B and 10B.

claim: Pk localization remained normal within A compartments of ft or ds mutants.
source: It could be that in the absence of Dachs and Ds, Sple is localized by the same cues that localize Pk, as Pk localization remained normal within A compartments of ft or ds mutants (Figure 8E,F,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 8E, 8F, and 8K.

claim: Mutation of dachs alone causes a reversal of hair polarity in P compartments of the abdomen.
source: However, mutation of dachs alone causes a reversal of hair polarity in P compartments (Figures 9B, 10B) (Matakatsu and Blair, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figures 9B and 10B, and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: The reversal of hair polarity in P compartments of dachs mutants is associated with a reversal of Pk localization.
source: This reversal of polarity is associated with a reversal of Pk localization (Figure 8G,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 8G and 8K.

claim: Pk localization is disturbed in P compartments of fat or ds mutants.
source: Pk localization is also disturbed in P compartments of fat or ds mutants (Figure 8E,F,K), as well as in fat dachs or ds dachs double mutants (Figure 8H,J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 8E, 8F, and 8K.

claim: Pk localization is disturbed in P compartments of fat dachs or ds dachs double mutants.
source: Pk localization is also disturbed in P compartments of fat or ds mutants (Figure 8E,F,K), as well as in fat dachs or ds dachs double mutants (Figure 8H,J,K).
evidence: This claim is supported by localization data shown in Figures 8H, 8J, and 8K.

claim: Interactions between Dachs and Sple, and between Ds and Sple, serve as a connection point between PCP pathways coordinating polarity in multiple Drosophila organs.
source: Our results implicate interactions between Dachs and Sple, and between Ds and Sple, as a connection point between PCP pathways coordinating polarity in multiple Drosophila organs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript showing physical interactions and functional relationships.

claim: The influence of Ds on Sple localization is essential for some manifestations of PCP, such as ommatidial polarity in the eye.
source: The influence of Ds on Sple localization is essential for some manifestations of PCP, such as ommatidial polarity in the eye.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Sple localization in the eye depends on Ds but not Dachs, and that Sple is required for ommatidial polarity.

claim: Localization of Sple by Ds could account for the long-range influence of Ds-Fat borders on PCP in the eye.
source: Indeed, because Fz PCP can propagate from cell to cell, we propose that localization of Sple by Ds could account for the long-range influence of Ds-Fat borders on PCP in the eye (Sharma and McNeill, 2013; Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Yang et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on the observed data and prior knowledge of Fz PCP propagation.

claim: The Sple isoform is not conserved in vertebrates.
source: While vertebrates have a Ds homologue that is required for PCP, Dchs1 (Mao et al., 2011a), Dchs1 must influence PCP in mammals through a distinct mechanism, as Pk is conserved in vertebrates, but the Sple isoform is not.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of vertebrate homologues and conservation patterns.

claim: Pk is conserved in vertebrates.
source: While vertebrates have a Ds homologue that is required for PCP, Dchs1 (Mao et al., 2011a), Dchs1 must influence PCP in mammals through a distinct mechanism, as Pk is conserved in vertebrates, but the Sple isoform is not.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of vertebrate homologues and conservation patterns.

claim: Ds-Fat signaling does not normally play a significant role in directing wing hair polarity.
source: However, since Ds-Fat signaling modulates Sple, but not Pk, localization, and Pk, but not Sple, is normally important for wing hair polarity, we infer that Ds-Fat PCP does not normally play a significant role in directing wing hair polarity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ds-Fat affects Sple but not Pk, and that Pk rather than Sple is important for wing hair polarity.

claim: The hair polarity phenotypes of ds or fat mutants are better understood as a de facto gain-of-function phenotype, resulting from inappropriate accumulation of Dachs on cell membranes.
source: Instead, we propose, as also suggested by (Blair, 2014), that the hair polarity phenotypes of ds or fat mutants are better understood as a de facto gain-of-function phenotype, resulting from inappropriate accumulation of Dachs on cell membranes, which then leads to inappropriate localization of Sple, and abnormal polarity.
evidence: This claim is a proposed interpretation of the data, supported by the observed effects of ds and fat mutations on Dachs and Sple localization.

claim: Uniform Ds expression can rescue hair polarity in ds fj mutants.
source: This would also explain how Ds-Fat signaling, stripped of polarizing information, could nonetheless rescue PCP phenotypes: for example, how uniform Ds expression can rescue hair polarity in ds fj mutants (Matakatsu and Blair, 2004; Simon, 2004), and how expression of the intracellular domain of Fat can rescue hair polarity in fat mutants (Matakatsu and Blair, 2006), as these manipulations suppress the membrane accumulation of Dachs that would otherwise occur in mutant animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Expression of the intracellular domain of Fat can rescue hair polarity in fat mutants.
source: This would also explain how Ds-Fat signaling, stripped of polarizing information, could nonetheless rescue PCP phenotypes: for example, how uniform Ds expression can rescue hair polarity in ds fj mutants (Matakatsu and Blair, 2004; Simon, 2004), and how expression of the intracellular domain of Fat can rescue hair polarity in fat mutants (Matakatsu and Blair, 2006), as these manipulations suppress the membrane accumulation of Dachs that would otherwise occur in mutant animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The effects of ds and fat mutants on microtubules within the wing are likely a consequence of abnormal Sple localization.
source: Thus, we propose that the effects of ds and fat mutants on microtubules within the wing are likely a consequence of abnormal Sple localization, which disrupts microtubule orientation, but need not be interpreted as evidence for a normal role of Ds-Fat signaling in orienting microtubules or Fz PCP in the wing.
evidence: This claim is a proposed interpretation based on the observed effects of ds and fat mutations on Sple localization and prior knowledge of Pk-Sple effects on microtubules.

claim: Feedback mechanisms enable cells to make a discrete choice between competing polarity signals.
source: The observation that cells sometimes need to choose between competing polarity signals leads us to emphasize that feedback mechanisms could also have a distinct, fundamentally important role in PCP that has not previously been considered – they enable cells to make a discrete choice between competing polarity signals.
evidence: This claim is a proposed interpretation based on the observed competition between Pk and Sple localization cues.

claim: Control of Sple localization is a key mechanism by which the Ds-Fat pathway coordinates with Fz to influence PCP.
source: Our results establish control of Sple localization as a key mechanism by which the Ds-Fat pathway coordinates with Fz to influence PCP, and enhance our understanding of how PCP is coordinated in developing tissues.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In some contexts PCP pathways operate in sequence, with directional information passed from Ds-Fat PCP to Fz PCP via Sple, whereas in other contexts they are uncoupled.
source: Thus, the solution our results support for the controversy over the relationship between the two PCP pathways is that in some contexts they operate in sequence, with directional information passed from Ds-Fat PCP to Fz PCP via Sple, whereas in other contexts they are uncoupled.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the organ-specific differences in PCP pathway interactions observed in the study.

claim: Mammalian homologues of Ds and Fat, Dchs1 and Fat4, influence PCP.
source: Mammalian homologues of Ds and Fat, Dchs1 and Fat4, also influence PCP (Mao et al., 2011a; Saburi et al., 2008; Zakaria et al., 2014), and human FAT4 can rescue PCP phenotypes of Drosophila fat mutants (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Human FAT4 can rescue PCP phenotypes of Drosophila fat mutants.
source: Mammalian homologues of Ds and Fat, Dchs1 and Fat4, also influence PCP (Mao et al., 2011a; Saburi et al., 2008; Zakaria et al., 2014), and human FAT4 can rescue PCP phenotypes of Drosophila fat mutants (Pan et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Fat protein in a cell within a Ds-Fj gradient preferentially accumulates along the side where it contacts cells with higher Ds and lower Fj.
source: Fat protein in a cell within a Ds-Fj gradient preferentially accumulates along the side where it contacts cells with higher Ds and lower Fj; Ds protein localizes in a complementary orientation (Figure 1A) (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Bosveld et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Ds protein localizes in a complementary orientation to Fat protein.
source: Fat protein in a cell within a Ds-Fj gradient preferentially accumulates along the side where it contacts cells with higher Ds and lower Fj; Ds protein localizes in a complementary orientation (Figure 1A) (Ambegaonkar et al., 2012; Bosveld et al., 2012; Brittle et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Polarization of Ds and Fat proteins establishes PCP in part through the unconventional myosin Dachs, whose membrane localization is regulated by Fat.
source: How polarization of Ds and Fat proteins establishes PCP is incompletely understood, but it is achieved in part through the unconventional myosin Dachs, whose membrane localization is regulated by Fat (Mao et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The Pk-Sple locus produces two functional isoforms: Prickle (Pk) and Spiny-legs (Sple), which share a common, LIM-domain containing C-terminus, but unique N-termini.
source: The Pk-Sple locus produces two functional isoforms: Prickle (Pk) and Spiny-legs (Sple), which share a common, LIM-domain containing C-terminus, but unique N-termini (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations that only affect pk disrupt PCP in the wing and notum, but not in the eye and leg.
source: These isoforms have distinct roles: for example, mutations that only affect pk disrupt PCP in the wing and notum, but not in the eye and leg, whereas mutations that only affect sple exhibit a complementary specificity.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from prior genetic studies.

claim: Mutations that only affect sple disrupt PCP in the eye and leg, but not in the wing and notum.
source: These isoforms have distinct roles: for example, mutations that only affect pk disrupt PCP in the wing and notum, but not in the eye and leg, whereas mutations that only affect sple exhibit a complementary specificity.
evidence: This claim is implied by the statement about complementary specificity of sple mutations compared to pk mutations.

claim: Mutations that affect both isoforms (pk-sple) have milder effects on PCP than isoform-specific alleles in the wing, notum, and leg.
source: The observations that mutations that affect both isoforms (pk-sple) have milder effects on PCP than isoform-specific alleles in the wing, notum, and leg, and that over-expression of Sple or Pk leads to PCP phenotypes reminiscent of loss-of-function of pk, or sple, respectively, led to the suggestion that a balance between Pk and Sple isoforms is necessary for normal PCP (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Over-expression of Sple or Pk leads to PCP phenotypes reminiscent of loss-of-function of pk, or sple, respectively.
source: The observations that mutations that affect both isoforms (pk-sple) have milder effects on PCP than isoform-specific alleles in the wing, notum, and leg, and that over-expression of Sple or Pk leads to PCP phenotypes reminiscent of loss-of-function of pk, or sple, respectively, led to the suggestion that a balance between Pk and Sple isoforms is necessary for normal PCP (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Pk expression is more abundant than Sple expression in larval wing discs.
source: Relative differences in expression of isoforms consistent with their distinct requirements have also been reported: Pk at higher levels than Sple in larval wing discs, and Sple at higher levels than Pk in eye discs (Ayukawa et al., 2014; Merkel et al., 2014; Olofsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sple expression is more abundant than Pk expression in eye discs.
source: Relative differences in expression of isoforms consistent with their distinct requirements have also been reported: Pk at higher levels than Sple in larval wing discs, and Sple at higher levels than Pk in eye discs (Ayukawa et al., 2014; Merkel et al., 2014; Olofsson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In sple mutants, ommatidial chirality is randomized.
source: In sple mutants, ommatidial chirality is randomized, whereas in pk mutant eyes ommatidial chirality is normal (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In pk mutant eyes, ommatidial chirality is normal.
source: In sple mutants, ommatidial chirality is randomized, whereas in pk mutant eyes ommatidial chirality is normal (Gubb et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: dachs mutation has little effect on fat PCP phenotypes in the eye.
source: Also, in contrast to the wing and abdomen, where dachs mutation suppresses fat PCP phenotypes, dachs mutation has little effect on fat PCP phenotypes in the eye (Brittle et al., 2012; Mao et al., 2006; Sharma and McNeill, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Suppression of pk polarity phenotypes by dachs was 100% penetrant.
source: Suppression of pk polarity phenotypes by dachs was 100% penetrant.
evidence: This claim is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.
